overview.text: A baseball home run (HR, or “homer”) is a fair-ball play on which the batter scores without being put out or benefiting from an error. Most often, the ball flies over the outfield fence in fair territory: the batter is credited with all four bases, and any runners already on base score as well. A ball that hits a foul pole counts. The ball need not leave the field, however: when it stays in play and the batter safely touches all four bases, it is an inside-the-park home run. Because one swing can score several runs, homers can sharply affect a game; they are also used to gauge hitting power, although park dimensions and conditions influence totals.

key_facts.text: A home run hit over the fence in fair territory gives the batter all four bases and scores any runners already on base.
A ball that hits a foul pole is a home run; foul poles mark the boundary between fair and foul territory.
An inside-the-park home run happens when a batter keeps the ball in play but safely reaches all four bases without being put out.
Home runs are used to evaluate hitters’ power, but ballpark size, wall height, and wind can affect whether a hit clears the fence.
Home-run records have been celebrated milestones: the Baseball Hall of Fame describes Babe Ruth’s 60 home runs in 1927 as a major benchmark, while noting that later players surpassed it.
